output.headline: Carers and drivers set for relief as Healey delivers first budget
output.bodyHtml:
John Healey will strike an optimistic note in his first budget on Wednesday, signalling “fresh hope for the future” and giving households breathing space from rising cost of living pressures, despite a turbulent international backdrop.

Healey insists he will put the country on a better path as he delivers his first budget, acknowledging that the UK faces a “difficult moment” against a turbulent global economic backdrop.

The budget will be read as a signal of Andy Burnham’s intent, though it is expected to be a relatively modest affair, with Healey putting off bigger decisions on tax and spending until next year amid stark fiscal realities.

“The world’s a highly uncertain place,” the chancellor said, in a video released before the budget. “Conflicts abroad are pushing up energy prices, and the cost of living here at home – piling pressure on the families, on businesses and on our public finances.”

Related: Budget 2026: six charts that reveal the economic realities facing the chancellor

Healey is expected to offer temporary support for poorer families ahead of a steep rise in typical energy bills in January, while pledging energy market reforms to bring bills down for all households in the longer term.

Andy Burnham has told MPs he is keen to abolish the gas standing charge – a fixed daily levy on all users – a move that would bring down bills for consumers who use less energy, with the cost picked up by those who use more.

As part of a series of “everyday fixes”, the chancellor is expected to end the carers’ allowance cliff edge – which has penalised unpaid carers for going over their earnings limit by as little as a few pence a week – and to cancel January’s planned increase in fuel duty.

Healey will announce plans to raise the minimum wage by nearly 4%, though he will slow the increase for under-21s after warnings that they were being priced out of jobs – a decision that has prompted accusations that Labour has broken a manifesto pledge.

He is also expected to protect pensioners and those saving for retirement, shielding nearly one million people from paying income tax, and is preparing to make the government’s revived Help to Buy scheme more generous, in a boost for middle earners.

Healey insisted the government would move to ease the cost of living “responsibly” by sticking to Labour’s self-imposed fiscal rules, as he attempts to reassure the markets that his plans for longer-term reform will make Britain “more resilient” from global shocks.

Cost-of-living measures are set to feature heavily in the budget, even though the chancellor has limited scope for big giveaways because of stretched public finances, made worse by international market turmoil from the Iran conflict.

In his pre-budget address, he added: “This budget is about getting through this difficult moment. But it’s also about putting Britain on a future path, a better future path.”

Industry experts fear that further investment in hydrogen and carbon capture will bear the brunt of efforts to rein in extra spending, a blow to the UK’s net zero targets.

The government has been under pressure to use the budget to set out a clear path for defence spending to hit 3% of national income by 2030 – a target Healey claimed to be committed to when he resigned as defence secretary earlier this year.

Healey is expected to confirm more investment in defence industries – described as a “downpayment” on hitting the target – though he will wait until next year’s spending review to confirm the timetable.

The budget will also set out a “roadmap” to devolving more tax revenues to local leaders in a significant shift towards moving spending power away from Whitehall to the regions and nations of the UK.

But the detail of Burnham’s devolution agenda in areas such as skills and employment support is not expected until the government publishes a white paper in the weeks ahead.

Cutting energy prices has the added benefit of bringing down inflation, helping to ease pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates. Markets are now expecting the Bank to hike rates four times, to 4.75%, over the next 12 months.

Healey is also expected to take action to offset part of the hit to the public finances from higher interest rates on government borrowing – the result of rising inflation and turmoil in global bond markets.

The government had to pay the highest yield, or interest rate, on new five-year bonds since 2008 on Tuesday, above 5%.

City analysts say bond market investors will be watching the budget closely – though the upward move in UK yields, or interest rates, have echoed those seen in other major economies.

The UK’s economy has proved more resilient than expected in the face of the Iran conflict but recent data has pointed to a deteriorating outlook.

At a cabinet meeting last week, Healey told ministers that rising inflation caused by the conflict, which hit an in-year high of 3.5% last month, was the political backdrop to the budget.

Consumer confidence has fallen at the fastest rate since Brexit; while the number of businesses in financial distress has hit its highest level in more than two decades, according to data published by consultancy BTG on Thursday, with hospitality and construction hardest hit.

Healey struck an optimistic note, however, saying: “Britain’s economy is showing real signs of resilience: investment’s up, productivity is growing and we had the joint fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of this year.”

Related: You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the books

To help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, Healey is poised to raise taxes for Britain’s banks, potentially reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt, which would raise upwards of £2bn a year. Online retailers will be responsible for collecting tax owed by firms selling on their platforms.

The Tories said the chancellor was set to “shy away” from the difficult decisions, including bringing down the welfare bill, which the prime minister has said he does not want to do through “crude cuts”.

The shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, Richard Fuller, said: “Britain’s public finances are on a cliff edge. A ‘do-nothing’ budget will not solve the problems staring us in the face: a spiralling welfare bill, a crippling tax burden, mounting debt and rising global threats.”

The Lib Dems warned against a “steady as she goes” budget. Their deputy leader, Daisy Cooper, said: “Families are being squeezed from all sides, businesses face mounting costs and for many it feels like even the basic joys in life have become unaffordable.”
output.standfirst: Healey is set to scrap the carers’ allowance cliff edge and cancel January’s fuel duty rise in his first budget, even as bigger decisions on tax and defence are deferred amid a strained economy, with the Tories accusing him of shying away from cutting welfare.
output.progress: Healey is also raising the minimum wage, shielding pensioners from income tax, and is poised to increase bank taxes to help offset the economic damage from the Middle East war.

output.headline: Energy secretary leans against Rosebank oilfield on climate grounds
output.bodyHtml:
Government insiders say the giant Rosebank oilfield can be approved without breaching the UK’s emission targets, a view that has strengthened the position of cabinet colleagues who are pushing for it to be given the go-ahead.

The Guardian revealed last week that Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, was leaning towards rejecting the project, but her position has put her at loggerheads with cabinet colleagues, including the chancellor, John Healey, who are lobbying for an approval.

Her allies say she is leaning away from approving the project because of the climate damage it would cause, which they argue is arguably not enough to breach legal limits but is not outweighed by the benefits that supporters of approval cite, including tax take, jobs and investment.

Government insiders have told the Guardian the project can be approved on a strict reading of Britain’s climate obligations, in part because once the oil is exported, the emissions from burning it no longer count against domestic targets. “Miatta has more latitude than you might think,” said one.

A decision to approve the oilfield would be met with dismay from climate campaigners and some Labour backbenchers who view it as a harmful step away from prioritising net zero – and may see the shift of emissions from one country to another as a trivial distinction.

On Tuesday, Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth wrote to the prime minister urging him to consider the cumulative impacts of big decisions on North Sea drilling, Heathrow expansion and grants for heat pumps – rather than viewing each in isolation.

But sources say the Treasury has already accounted for billions of pounds’ worth of tax revenue from Rosebank and so would be faced with a shortfall should it be rejected.

“The climate case against was never the direct emissions,” one source said. “Instead it was the leadership position … the power of a G7 producer seeking to put that into action is the climate point, not the direct emissions.”

Related: Rosebank row: will Labour block the oilfield? – podcast

Greg Muttitt, a climate researcher at University College, London, said the government was wrong to approve the Jackdaw gasfield last week and would be wrong to approve Rosebank, which would generate around seven times the emissions.

But he added: “It is true that the UK government is not going to find itself in any international court if it approves Rosebank. Approving it is not inconsistent with what the UK has committed to firmly, because most of the oil will be exported and so will count towards other countries’ emissions.”

Fahnbulleh has been forced to make a decision over Rosebank because of a legal judgment that the previous environmental consent was incorrectly given by the Conservative government at the time.

A judge ruled in 2024 that ministers should have accounted for emissions not just from drilling for oil at Rosebank, but also from those which will be generated by burning it.

Given most of that oil will be burned abroad, however, the resulting emissions will not count against the UK’s carbon budgets. Experts estimate that Rosebank could emit 1m additional tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2042, against an overall limit of 90m tonnes.

Related: Andy Burnham vows UK will hit net zero target despite Jackdaw gasfield approval

Fahnbulleh is under an obligation to take into account Britain’s commitment under the Paris agreement to take action to prevent global temperatures rising more than 1.5C.

In her decision to approve the Jackdaw scheme last week, however, she noted Jackdaw would account for about 0.01% of global greenhouse gas emissions created by the oil and gas industry in 2035.

Some experts believe Rosebank could be approved without meaningfully adding to global temperature changes. But others insist that any new oil and gasfields are harmful to the goal of staying within safe carbon budgets.

Downing Street insiders insist the decision rests with Fahnbulleh, rather than with Andy Burnham. However supportive ministers have interpreted the prime minister’s promise to take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas as a signal he would support giving the green light to Rosebank.

He has also talked of “reindustrialisation” in a speech in Motherwell, North Lanarkshire, this month, language often associated in Scotland with the North Sea. Scottish Labour MPs are believed to be overwhelmingly in favour of approving the oilfield.

Fahnbulleh told the Guardian last week that while she had approved the Jackdaw gasfield on the grounds of national energy security, the same concerns did not necessarily apply to Rosebank.

In recent days, people close to the chancellor have said he wants Fahnbulleh to approve the project.

The Guardian has learned that part of the reason for this is the Treasury has already accounted for the tax benefits, which Adura, the company operating the field, estimate would be £500m a year by the end of this parliament.

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Any decision will be made through the quasi-judicial process, taking into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received as part of the regulatory process.”
output.standfirst: Her allies say Miatta Fahnbulleh is leaning against approval because of the climate damage it would cause, despite cabinet pressure and government insiders insisting a yes would not breach the UK's emissions targets.
output.progress: Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth have written to the prime minister, urging him to weigh the climate impact of Rosebank alongside Heathrow expansion and heat pump policy.

output.headline: Bot-detection checks safeguard outcome of UK’s vape ban consultation
output.bodyHtml:
The Department of Health and Social Care excluded the 90,835 automated responses from its decision-making, and Keir Starmer’s Labour government went on to inherit the tobacco and vapes bill in 2024 and pass it into law, including the ban on businesses selling or supplying disposable vapes.

AI bots had flooded the government consultation with tens of thousands of fake responses in a failed attempt to stop the UK’s ban on disposable vapes.

Three-quarters of all the responses to the 2023 consultation on the tobacco and vapes bill were machine-generated, in what is thought to be the first coordinated attempt to use AI to derail health policymaking in the UK.

The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) used bot-detection methods to identify that 90,835 of the 118,756 responses it received, 76%, were submitted by bots.

The attempt to manipulate the outcome of the consultation was disclosed on Tuesday in research published in the journal Tobacco Control by the health policy experts Dr Nason Maani, from the University of Edinburgh, and Prof Anna Gilmore, of the University of Bath.

All but two of those 90,835 automated responses answered the same question in the “smoke free generation” consultation, in which they opposed Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government’s plan to ban disposable vapes. The submissions were “often duplicated many times and sent at high frequency from a small number of IP addresses”, the DHSC said.

The bombardment “appears to be the first documented instance of large-scale automated interference in a formal public health policy consultation”, the researchers said.

Maani added that while this attempt was identified, “the threat is that future campaigns become harder to catch, and what we can’t catch, we don’t know about. Such campaigns are a threat because they raise the possibility of a handful of powerful interests looking like a mass movement.”

Caroline Cerny, the deputy chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said: “Evidence that AI bots have been used to swamp a Department of Health consultation is deeply concerning.

“Given the tobacco industry’s history of seeking to undermine public health regulation, we need to be alert to the risk that technological advances can be used to further commercial interests around health policy and put safeguards in place.

“Decisions that affect public health must be based on sound evidence and expertise, not manipulated response numbers.”

Related: More than 6m vapes and pods discarded weekly in UK despite single-use ban, study finds

Azzurra Moores, the associate director for information ecosystems at the thinktank Demos, described the attempt to derail the ban as “pretty alarming”.

“Public consultations are one of the main ways government opens up its decision-making, so any interference with them is a serious concern,” she said. “These findings are pretty alarming: if a consultation can be swamped like this, it stops telling policymakers what the public actually thinks and undermines trust in the process.

“This is a problem without easy answers. Every barrier that keeps bots out also makes it harder for real people to take part, and AI makes fake responses far harder to spot. Interference can adapt faster than departments can update their checks. Better screening and more transparency will help, but there’s no single fix.”

The DHSC said its “robust controls” identified the attempt to influence the consultation.

A spokesperson said: “We always have robust controls in place to prevent the manipulation of our public consultations, and those controls worked effectively in this case.

“As a result, the fake responses were removed, and the consultation helped inform the landmark action we are taking to create a smoke-free generation.

“We will remain alert to interference of this kind in future consultation processes, and we will not be deterred from doing what is necessary to promote healthier living.”
output.standfirst: The Department of Health’s bot-detection checks caught and excluded 90,835 machine-generated responses opposing the ban, after AI was used in what researchers call the first coordinated attempt to derail UK health policymaking.
output.progress: The Department of Health and Social Care’s bot-detection checks caught and excluded 90,835 fake automated responses before the ban was decided.

output.headline: Sizewell C construction presses on with over 2,000 workers on site
output.bodyHtml:
A government spokesperson said: 'Once operational, Sizewell C could save £2bn a year across the energy system, cutting costs for families up and down the country, and the project is already making good progress with over 2,000 workers on site.'

The government's spending watchdog said the plan to fund a multibillion-pound nuclear plant at the Sizewell site in Suffolk amounts to a 'terrible deal' for the UK taxpayer over the rest of the century.

MPs on the public accounts committee (PAC) have warned that the cost of the Sizewell C nuclear reactor could spiral to almost £48bn, leaving bill payers to provide an extra £9.8bn to construct the plant before 2040 and a further £12bn over its 60-year operating life.

The government spokesperson said the report 'completely ignores that investors are incentivised to complete construction as cheaply and quickly as possible' through the terms of the deal.

Taxpayers and consumers face a 'high level of risk', according to PAC, after the government agreed to take a near-45 per cent stake in the nuclear plant, which is considered a successor project to the heavily delayed Hinkley Point C nuclear plant in Somerset.

Related: Spending watchdog warns £38bn cost of Sizewell C nuclear plant is 'risky'

Under the terms of the multibillion-pound deal, which will be paid for through taxes and energy bills, the UK government holds a 44.9 per cent stake while French state nuclear developer EDF has a 12.5 per cent stake.

The rest of the funding has come from private investors including the British Gas owner Centrica, which holds a 15 per cent share, alongside the Canadian investment group La Caisse, which holds 20 per cent, and the investment manager Amber Infrastructure, which has a 7.6 per cent stake.

The UK government was forced to take a larger than expected share of the project after buying out Chinese state nuclear developer CGN, which had been allowed to hold a 20 per cent stake in Sizewell C before national security concerns emerged.

The watchdog warned that while the British public could be called on to shoulder multibillion-pound cost overruns, the nuclear project's private investors would only need to put in an extra £30m.

Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the PAC chair, said: 'The high level of risk borne by taxpayers and consumers for the construction of Sizewell C is extraordinary. Private investors look set for significant returns on their investments, while customers are likely to be saddled with higher energy bills.'

He urged the government to 'focus on the successful delivery of this project', and in building confidence in the UK's nuclear industry more broadly, so that taxpayers will 'never be put in this position again'.

The government expects Sizewell C to cost between £40.5bn and £47.7bn and to complete construction between 2039 and 2043. The committee has called on the government to provide the scenario analysis it used to underpin its cost estimates for the project within the next three months, and asked ministers to provide an update on the project's development every six months to keep track of its progress.

Tom Greatrex, the chief executive of the Nuclear Industry Association, said Sizewell C would provide 'clean, reliable and constantly available power' that could save households billions from paying the cost of balancing the grid or building extra network connections.

'Currently, the consumer is footing a bill of £2.8bn so far this year to manage a dysfunctional grid, paying both for wind to stop generating at some times, and for gas-powered backup at others,' he said.

Critics of the project, including Alison Downes of the Stop Sizewell C campaign group and Prof Steve Thomas of Greenwich Business School, who provided joint evidence to the committee, have suggested that the cost of abandoning the project today would be lower than the cost of paying inflated energy bills over 60 years 'multiple times over'.

They called on the government to rule out using this funding model for future nuclear projects. 'All it offers is a free ride for investors and financial pain for households,' they said in a joint statement.
output.standfirst: Construction continues at the Sizewell C nuclear plant, with more than 2,000 workers already on site, as the public accounts committee says taxpayers face an 'extraordinary' risk from a cost that could reach almost £48bn.
output.progress: More than 2,000 workers are already building the plant, and ministers say the deal's terms incentivise investors to finish it quickly and cheaply.

output.headline: Jury convicts former Met officer, Met says justice has been done
output.bodyHtml:
Mark Tyrrell, a former Metropolitan police officer who served in the same specialist unit as Sarah Everard’s killer, Wayne Couzens, has been convicted of one count of rape, three of sexual assault and one of perverting the course of justice, following a trial at Southwark crown court.

Ch Supt Sara Leach, commander within specialist operations, said: “This kind of conduct is abhorrent but even more so when it is carried out by a serving officer, who had gained the trust of the victim.

“We remain appalled that someone like this was serving within our organisation and it is right he has been brought to justice.”

Tyrrell was found guilty of sexual offences against a woman he met through his work as an officer, who cannot be identified for legal reasons.

A court heard that Tyrrell raped the woman by having sex with her after she repeatedly said no.

The 57-year-old was then said to have told her “I don’t believe what’s just happened” and “do you realise that what I’ve just done, that was rape?”

Tyrrell had been attached to the parliamentary and diplomatic protection command, which is where the convicted rapists Couzens and David Carrick both worked.

Prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC alleged that when the woman resisted Tyrrell’s sexual advances “he simply chose to take what he wanted”.

The court heard that concerns were raised after officers attended her address for a separate matter and found Tyrrell hiding by the side of her bed.

The former PC was found guilty of perverting the course of justice by attempting to delete messages with the woman.

In one message, the court was told he said he was “sorry” for “being a sex offender” and “for ruining your life by being in it”.

Jurors found him not guilty in relation to 13 other charges, including one count of rape.

In his evidence, Tyrrell claimed sexual intercourse between them was always consensual and “there was never any forcefulness to it”.

Tyrrell previously admitted misconduct in a public office. He also pleaded guilty to perverting the course of justice by persuading the woman to lie to the police about why he was in her bedroom.

The defendant, of Meltham, West Yorkshire, will be sentenced on 16 December.

Everard, 33, was kidnapped, raped and murdered by then Met officer Couzens in 2021. He was later given a whole-life order.

Carrick, 51, who previously served as an armed officer in the Met, is serving 37 life sentences after attacking more than a dozen women.

  • Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html
output.standfirst: The Met says justice has been done after a jury convicted Mark Tyrrell, who served alongside Sarah Everard's murderer Wayne Couzens and serial rapist David Carrick, of rape and sexual assault
output.progress: The Metropolitan police says it is right that Tyrrell has been convicted and brought to justice for abusing his position of trust.

output.headline: Judge cancels Flávio Bolsonaro's passport as lawmakers seek his arrest
output.bodyHtml:
A supreme court justice moved to cancel the passport of the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro within minutes of Sunday’s election result, part of a criminal case examining a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies. He missed Tuesday’s 11am deadline to hand the document to federal police, and several Brazilian news organisations reported that he had instead fled the country for the United States after losing the presidential election to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who called the act “shameful”.

A report by the news website Metrópoles, citing people close to the politician’s family, said he was en route to the US. “The plane is in flight,” Metrópoles reported, without making clear where it had departed from.

Bolsonaro allies told Metrópoles that he would land in Florida on Tuesday afternoon and planned to request political asylum. “The Donald Trump administration has been informed,” the website added.

Lula condemned Bolsonaro’s apparent decision to flee. “This is what the family Bolsonaro are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as he’s become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.

“I keep imagining what’s on the conscience of a citizen who just lost the elections and flees his country … He who owes nothing, fears nothing. A citizen who sneaks out of his country owes something. The act of leaving Brazil is shameful.”

Allies also confirmed to the Folha de S Paulo newspaper that Bolsonaro was on his way to the US, and said the escape plan had been “organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan”.

“They say the flight should land in a few hours,” the newspaper added.

The news network CNN Brasil reported that Bolsonaro had fled to the US with his wife and two daughters in the early hours of this morning.

A US state department spokesperson said Bolsonaro and his family would be granted visas “to allow them entry into the United States”.

Lawmakers from Lula’s Workers’ party asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s arrest and requested that his name be put on Interpol’s Red Notice list.

Bolsonaro had not been seen since Monday and missed a Tuesday-morning deadline to hand his passport to the federal police, fuelling rumours that he may have fled Brazil after losing on Sunday.

A report in the Brazilian newspaper O Globo said that during a meeting with friends and lawyers on Monday, the defeated candidate had appeared “possessed and made it clear he was afraid of being arrested”.

A supreme court justice cancelled Bolsonaro’s passport minutes after the result in a ruling related to a criminal case against the senator. He had until 11am to surrender the document to the federal police, but did not appear.

Bolsonaro has had Italian citizenship since 2023 and reportedly possesses a passport from the European country.

The Argentinian news website Infobae reported that on Monday night he reportedly fled to Argentina, where he was expected to board a private jet in Puerto Iguazú bound for the US, but the plane did not take off.

Related: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede defeat to Lula, posted a video on Monday in which, commenting on the cancellation of his passport, he said: “I never thought about leaving the country.”

One of the senator’s brothers, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, who is in self-imposed exile in the US, had said in an interview last Friday that his brother should leave Brazil if he lost.

The Brazilian newspaper Folha de S Paulo reported that allies in the Bolsonaro family’s inner circle had been told that he had indeed left for Argentina and intended to travel from there to the US.

As there is no record of him passing through any regular Brazilian immigration checkpoint, the federal police are trying to establish from Argentinian authorities whether there is any record of him entering the country.

The Argentinian channel Todo Noticias reported that the senator had reportedly crossed the border into Argentina on foot and abandoned plans to board the plane once news of his movements leaked.

Bolsonaro was told to surrender his passport over a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating him for possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies.

The senator’s possible flight makes the future of the far right after the presidential election even more uncertain. The family patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest for attempting a coup, and one of his sons is in the US and the whereabouts of another unclear.

Eduardo Bolsonaro has an outstanding arrest warrant against him in Brazil, after being sentenced to four years in prison for trying to interfere in his father’s trial by lobbying Donald Trump to impose sanctions on the justices hearing the case.

Political scientist Magna Inácio, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais, believes a power vacuum may now emerge within the right.

“The resistance of Brazilian voters to handing victory to this more extremist camp sends a signal that the right leadership is now up for grabs,” she said.

Since Jair Bolsonaro, then a career congressman with few laws to his name, surprisingly won the presidency in 2018, there has effectively been no right wing in Brazil, only the far-right Bolsonarismo movement.

Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, believes the fact that three Bolsonaros are now potentially out of the picture could trigger a “shift in power” away from blood ties.

“I think there is a tendency for power to move away from the sons,” said Rocha, noting that before the election, polls showed Jair Bolsonaro supporters preferred other potential candidates over his eldest son, including Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was recently elected senator, and the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas.

Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly did not want to run because he thought a presidential campaign would turn his life into “hell”, and believed his re-election to the senate was assured. But with Eduardo, his father’s “plan A”, now living in the US, the senator was chosen to run.

Most observers agree that Flávio lacks his father’s charisma. He had a 24-year political career in which he passed very few laws as a state legislator and senator, and the only previous time he ran for executive office was for mayor of Rio de Janeiro in 2016, when he fainted during a televised debate and finished fourth.

Speaking in Brasília, Bolsonaro’s campaign chief, senator Rogério Marinho, said he was surprised by reports of his candidate’s departure. “Because yesterday we talked about the need for Flávio, with the 60 million votes he received, to take on this role as leader of the opposition … since we were given a mandate by a significant part of the population,” he said.

Asked whether he believed Bolsonaro could lead the opposition from abroad, he said: “María Corina Machado did it” with her country, Venezuela.

Even in a family frequently embroiled in legal trouble he stood out, facing longstanding criminal allegations, including suspicions that he embezzled part of his staff’s salaries, as well as more recent accusations.

Even so, 48.21% of Brazilians voted for Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, which many analysts see as both an anti-Lula vote and a vote for whomever Jair Bolsonaro had chosen.

Inácio believes the struggle over the Bolsonaro legacy will also play out among family members who remain in Brazil, including Michelle and Bolsonaro’s other political sons, the senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro and congressman-elect Jair Renan Bolsonaro, who publicly do not get along with their stepmother.

“Michelle clearly has a political project of her own, but she is likely to face strong resistance from the two stepsons who are in congress. It is only a matter of time before tensions between them grow,” said the political scientist.
output.standfirst: A supreme court justice cancelled the senator’s passport and Workers’ party lawmakers have asked for his arrest, after he reportedly fled to Argentina and then the US following his election defeat by Lula.
output.progress: A supreme court justice, federal police and Workers’ party lawmakers are all acting on the senator’s missed passport deadline and the money-laundering case against him.

output.headline: Commonwealth summit to put slavery’s legacy on the agenda, Charles confirms
output.bodyHtml:
King Charles has confirmed he will discuss the legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at a summit next week, as he begins his Caribbean tour.

The king arrived in the Bahamas to a ceremonial welcome and attended a youth rally at Clifford Park, the site where the country officially gained its independence from British colonial rule in 1973.

His visit comes amid renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for the atrocities of transatlantic slavery and engage in reparations talks.

Charles’s nine-day tour, which includes a solo state visit to Guyana, will culminate in presiding over the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) hosted by Antigua and Barbuda.

In his speech in the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles said: “Some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness.

“It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future.”

He said the Chogm leaders would discuss matters relating to the legacy of slavery next week in Antigua.

Charles acknowledged the “appalling atrocity of slavery”, describing it as something “which forever stains our history, when he attended the ceremony marking Barbados’s historic transition to a republic in 2021.

A year later he described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to “deepen my own understanding of slavery’s enduring impact”, in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: “At the request of host governments, the king’s programme will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future that are having a transformative effect on the region, as it confronts the challenges of today.

“For his majesty, this tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past. This will therefore also be reflected in differing ways and words during the tour, as you would expect.”

But a statement from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee said the king’s comments on Tuesday “fall short of what justice requires”.

“Our culture is not born out of darkness; our culture was born out of agency and out of the will to survive despite the horrors, trauma and degradation. Our culture is a testament to the power of the human spirit, not simply a reaction to the worst examples of it.

“We therefore do not need King Charles to tell us how outstanding our culture is … We need him to speak about his role in the darkness and how he plans to atone for it actively.

“The royal family and the British government were responsible for the darkness. His comments fall short of what justice requires – a full and formal apology – and they do not speak to the steps needed to remedy the wrongs committed in the name of the crown he wears.”

Dr Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the committee’s chair, told the Guardian that while she appreciated the king’s attempt to “connect with Bahamian culture” in his speech his words felt “like hollow platitudes”.

She added: “I am very proud of my Bahamian people and the beautiful spirit and hospitality that they shared. My critique is not an attempt to rain on their parade. It is because of this pride that I feel we deserve so much more than what was offered.”

Related: King Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summit

The chair of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, Prof Hilary Beckles, said what the Caribbean was looking for was “proprietary justice, beginning with remorse”.

Beckles added that when speaking to Caribbean young people the king should “dig deep within his consciousness” and give to them “the empowerment that he would give to his own children” to survive in a rapidly changing world. Anything short of that would be to condone and minimise the legacy of harm and suffering that continues today, he said.

Charles is to travel to Guyana on Thursday where the president, Mohamed Irfaan Ali, recently called for the monarch to take the next step and offer to apologise.

The king follows the guidance of his ministers, and it is understood the government has not advised him to offer an apology or reparations, in keeping with established policy.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, will join Charles in Antigua for the gathering of Commonwealth leaders.

Additional reporting by Press Association

output.headline: Fleetwood write new history with penalty shootout win over Arsenal
output.bodyHtml:
Fleetwood Town pulled off one of the greatest upsets in English football history, beating Arsenal on penalties in the Carabao Cup at a stadium that happens to share its name with Highbury, where Arsenal last played more than 20 years ago. It was the team in red shirts and white sleeves that triumphed this time, though not the one many would have predicted.

Fleetwood battled to the end after Aaron Loupalo-Bi and Viktor Gyökeres had exchanged goals in normal time, holding firm even as Arsenal dominated without finding a winner. Home manager Matt Lawlor was almost in tears with relief when Conor Haughey smashed home the decisive penalty to settle the shootout.

Related: Fleetwood Town stun Arsenal on penalties: Carabao Cup fourth round – live

Before that, goalkeeper Jay Lynch – a former warehouse worker – had saved from Brazil international Bruno Guimarães, exactly the kind of storyline football fans crave but so rarely get in the sanitised modern game.

Fleetwood had been set to earn £400,000 from the night but got something priceless instead: everyone in the ground will never forget watching the fourth-tier side knock out the Premier League champions. They rode their luck, helped by Max Dowman’s debatable sending-off, but football is rarely about logic – it is about emotion, and this was a once-in-a-lifetime night for the Cod Army, and anyone at their level, that they thoroughly enjoyed.

Lawlor’s rise has been remarkable: a year ago he was not even a football manager, having never played professionally, and began his coaching career with the Manchester United Foundation. Lynch, too, spent much of his early career in non-league, once only able to dream of playing a team that had narrowly lost the Champions League final in the spring.

Few predicted anything but a routine Arsenal win, even with Mikel Arteta giving several youngsters the chance to impress. Loupalo-Bi, on loan from Fulham, made the most of his opportunity, exposing the inexperience of 17-year-old Marli Salmon.

Loupalo-Bi, who has been learning his trade in the fourth tier this season, used his strength against the defender, spinning away from Salmon before slotting the ball under goalkeeper Illan Meslier to spark wild celebrations for the second time that night.

By that point the game had already survived a six-minute delay after a drone was flown above the pitch, with referee Michael Salisbury taking the players to the sidelines while police searched for the culprit outside the ground. It was an unusual start to what became an extraordinary night on the Fylde Coast, one that had begun with a flurry of pyrotechnics sending a red haze across the pitch that, frankly, never quite lifted, literally or metaphorically.

Fleetwood’s disciplined defence, well organised by Lawlor and his staff, made the first half a toil for Arsenal, repeatedly thwarting a Gunners side unable to create anything meaningful. Kai Havertz had the best chance to equalise before the break but headed wide, summing up a difficult afternoon for the striker.

After the break, Martin Ødegaard came on and became Arsenal’s quarterback, bringing the cohesion and intensity the Gunners had sorely lacked and helping drag them back into the game.

Gyökeres bundled home the equaliser, and few would have doubted Arsenal going on to win from there – but Fleetwood held firm.

The home side had been direct from the start, accepting their limitations and trusting the conditions to help them: a swirling wind kept the ball up in the air and unsettled Arsenal’s defenders, who were unused to the gales off the sea.

Fleetwood’s robust approach needled Arsenal, and Dowman was wound up into reacting to Fleetwood’s enforcer-in-chief, Harrison Neal, and was sent off – the second Gunners teenager to learn a hard lesson about life outside the top flight, after Salmon was caught out for the goal.

It may have been harsh, but it was needlessly petulant from Dowman on an already difficult night for his side. Mikel Arteta had a word with him on the way off. What did Arteta say? ‘Something that we discussed already before the match.’

Arsenal had two late chances, through Ben White and Gyökeres, to avoid the lottery of penalties, but Lynch produced two fantastic saves as the clock passed 90 minutes, setting up a fittingly dramatic finale in which he would be the hero again, on a great night for football and for the town of Fleetwood.
output.standfirst: Fourth-tier Fleetwood, managed by a coach who was not in football a year ago, held firm until Jay Lynch's save and Conor Haughey's winning penalty sent the Premier League champions out of the Carabao Cup.
